title: Patch One Machine Before the Worm Spreads
statement:
A network has n machines. graph is an n × n matrix where graph[i][j] = 1 means machines i and j are directly linked (links work both ways, and graph[i][i] = 1).

The machines listed in initial carry a worm. The worm spreads along links: any machine linked to an infected one gets infected, and this repeats until nothing changes.

Before the spread starts you may clean exactly one machine from initial. Cleaning does not unplug it: it stays in the network and can be infected again by a neighbour. Return the machine to clean so that the final number of infected machines is as small as possible. If several choices tie, return the smallest index.

examples.why: Cleaning 0 keeps both 0 and 1 healthy, 2 machines saved. Cleaning 2 saves only machine 2.
Machines 1 and 2 share a group, so cleaning one of them is pointless: the other reinfects it. Cleaning 3 saves the group {3, 4}.
Each choice saves one machine. On a tie, return the smaller index, not the first one listed.

constraints: graph[i][j] is 0 or 1, graph[i][j] = graph[j][i], graph[i][i] = 1
All values in initial are distinct
hints: The worm takes over whole connected groups. Think in groups, not machines.
Cleaning a machine only helps if no other infected machine shares its group. In that case, how many machines does it save?

Find the groups with union-find or DFS, count group sizes and how many initial machines sit in each. Among initial machines that are alone in their group, pick the one whose group is largest, with ties to the smaller index. If none is alone, return the smallest index in initial.

explain.intuition:
Once one machine in a connected group is infected, the whole group falls. So the final damage is the total size of all groups that contain at least one infected machine.

Cleaning machine m changes that only if m is the only infected machine in its group. Then the whole group is saved. If another infected machine shares the group, it reinfects m and nothing is saved. So the best choice is the lone infected machine in the largest group. If no machine is alone, every choice saves nothing, and the tie rule picks the smallest index in initial.
steps: Group the machines with union-find over every graph[i][j] = 1 link, or with DFS.
Count the size of each group and how many initial machines it contains.
For each machine in initial whose group has exactly one infected machine, its saving is the group size.
Return the machine with the largest saving, breaking ties by smaller index. If no saving is positive, return min(initial).
pitfalls: Treating cleaning as removing the machine from the network. Here it stays and can be reinfected, so a group with two infected machines cannot be saved.
Returning initial[0] on ties. initial is not sorted; the rule is the smallest index.
Picking the biggest infected group regardless of how many infected machines it holds, as in example 2.

solutions.title: Simulate every choice
solutions.idea: For each candidate, spread the worm from the other initial machines with BFS and count the damage.
solutions.time: O(k · n²) for k initial machines

solutions.title: Union-find: lone infected machine in the largest group
solutions.idea: Only a machine that is the single infected one in its group saves anything, and it saves the whole group.

followups: Now cleaning a machine removes it from the network entirely, links and all. Why does the group-counting shortcut no longer work directly?
You may clean two machines. How does the answer change?
